title: Mid-December, still a quiet week
intro: This week sits in mid-December. Little goes into the ground. Plant garlic or shallots only if the soil crumbles. Pick winter crops, and keep food and a water dish usable in a frost.

sow.name: Garlic in the south, if the soil allows
sow.detail: December is still a planting month in the south, and only in workable soil. The northern list does not include December. The next northern month is February. Frozen or waterlogged ground can wait in both regions.

sow.name: Shallot sets in the south, if the soil allows
sow.detail: The same rule as garlic this week: south only, and only where the soil crumbles. Sit each set with the tip just showing. The northern list starts in February.

sow.name: No outdoor sowing
sow.detail: There is nothing useful to sow outdoors in this list in December. Leave the packets. Pots under cover for beans and peas wait until February in the south, and later in the north.

sow.name: A windowsill tray
sow.detail: Pea shoots or cress on a bright sill are the green picking that does not need the garden. Sow a new tray when you cut the old one.

harvest.name: Leeks
harvest.detail: Lift as you cook them. They are in the harvest list for both regions through winter. Leave the rest of the row standing.

harvest.name: Parsnips
harvest.detail: Still in the ground. Lift after frost if you can get onto the bed without smearing it. Keep the row marked.

harvest.name: Brussels sprouts and kale
harvest.detail: Pick sprouts from the bottom upwards, and kale a few leaves at a time. Both are December crops in the south and the north.

harvest.name: Swede
harvest.detail: December is a harvest month in the south, and in the north through January. Lift what you will eat and leave the rest.

birds.name: Short days
birds.detail: Fill hanging feeders in the morning so there is food before the long night. Robins, blackbirds, blue tits and great tits are the usual birds at a winter feeder.

birds.name: Tits and starlings
birds.detail: Sunflower hearts, and suet if the cold keeps it firm. Starlings will finish a suet block quickly. Put out what you can replace while it is fresh.

birds.name: Fieldfares, redwings and blackcaps
birds.detail: Halved apples on the lawn for the thrushes. A blackcap may also take suet from a hanging feeder. These are winter visitors or winter feeders, not a reason to put a nest box up this week.

birds.name: Water
birds.detail: Break ice each morning, and again later if you are there. A little warm water helps you free a dish. Do not add salt, antifreeze or glycerine.

food.name: Sunflower hearts
food.detail: The straightforward seed for tits, finches and sparrows. Keep the bag dry and the feeder no fuller than the birds will finish.

food.name: Suet only while it is firm
food.detail: Useful in a frost. Take it down in a mild spell, when it softens and can smear on feathers.

food.name: Apples
food.detail: Sound fruit, halved, on the ground, for thrushes and blackcaps. Not a plate of leftover cooked food, which can be salty or spoiled.

food.name: Smaller amounts
food.detail: Rain and frost both spoil a feeder that was filled for the week. Top up in the morning with what will be eaten.

also: Do not dig soil that smears. Spread compost only where you will not be walking.
Wash a feeder that smells sour before you refill it.
Check fruit, potatoes and onions in store, and remove anything rotten.
Net winter brassicas if pigeons are in them, and peg the net to the ground.
Use the week to plan 2027: which bed is free, which crop you actually eat, and which month the planner gives it.
